desc: Sinatra's concept album of after-hours heartbreak, arranged by Nelson Riddle.
Sibling harmonies on traditional murder ballads and songs of sin, death and loss.
Debut album mixing rockabilly, R&B covers and country, including Blue Suede Shoes.
Sinatra's breezy swing set of love standards with Nelson Riddle's brassy arrangements.
Louis Prima, Keely Smith and Sam Butera's band in a rowdy Vegas lounge-act medley style.
Live festival set famed for Paul Gonsalves's marathon tenor solo on Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue.
Buddy Holly's band debut with hiccupping vocals and tight guitar, including That'll Be the Day.
Debut collecting Little Richard's screaming, piano-pounding hits such as Tutti Frutti and Long Tall Sally.
Rolling boogie piano and relaxed vocals from Fats Domino, including Blueberry Hill.
Percussion-led Blue Note session by Sabu Martinez with Arsenio Rodriguez on tres.
Compiled nonet sessions with soft, layered arrangements that defined the cool jazz sound.
Monk's angular compositions with Sonny Rollins, including a notoriously difficult title track.
Solo acoustic folk songs and cowboy ballads in the Woody Guthrie tradition.
Tito Puente's horn-driven mambo and cha-cha dance record from the Palladium era.
Machito's orchestra blending Afro-Cuban rhythm with jazz soloists including Cannonball Adderley.
Sarah Vaughan live in a small Chicago club, loose and improvisational with her trio.
Tight, powerful big band swing built on Neal Hefti's arrangements, including Li'l Darlin'.
Late Billie Holiday recording, her worn voice set against lush string arrangements.
Introductory raga performances with Shankar explaining Indian classical music to Western listeners.
One side of big band swing, one side of string-backed ballads.
Expansive set of Gershwin songs with Nelson Riddle's orchestral arrangements.
Story songs of outlaws and the Old West, including El Paso.
Quartet record built on unusual time signatures, including Take Five.
Sextet session of spare, modal improvisations with Coltrane, Adderley and Bill Evans.
Brotherly two-part harmonies over rock and roll, country and teen ballads.
Elvis's first album after army service, mixing blues, ballads and rock and roll.
Debut of traditional ballads sung in a clear soprano over spare acoustic guitar.
Live festival set from Muddy Waters's band, including Got My Mojo Working.
US debut presenting South African songs in several languages, including Xhosa click songs.
Live club recording known for conversational interplay between Evans and bassist Scott LaFaro.
Ray Charles reworks country standards with strings and big band, including I Can't Stop Loving You.
Early American bossa nova record pairing Getz's tenor with Byrd's nylon-string guitar.
Stax house band's organ-led instrumental debut, built around the title track.
Concept album of barroom heartache led by the Willie Nelson-penned title track.
Dylan's second album of protest and love songs, including Blowin' in the Wind.
Blues-soaked organ grooves from Jimmy Smith with Stanley Turrentine on tenor.
Live Harlem set capturing James Brown's revue at full intensity, with nonstop transitions.
Second Beatles album mixing originals with Motown and rock and roll covers.
Phil Spector's Wall of Sound Christmas album featuring the Ronettes, Crystals and Darlene Love.
Mingus's multi-part ballet suite with dense, emotionally volatile orchestration.
Dusty Springfield's solo debut of soul-influenced pop songs, including Bacharach material.
Compilation of Solomon Burke's early Atlantic soul sides, including Cry to Me.
Ferocious live set backed by the Nashville Teens in a Hamburg club.
Debut album made largely of R&B and blues covers.
Live Paris concert capturing Brel's intensely theatrical chanson performances, including Amsterdam.
First Beatles album of all original songs, tied to their debut film.
Soft bossa nova collaboration including The Girl from Ipanema with Astrud Gilberto.
Bright, trebly Bakersfield country built on twangy guitar and close harmony.
Fully electric Dylan album opening with Like a Rolling Stone, closing with Desolation Row.
Half electric, half acoustic; Dylan's first move toward rock with band accompaniment.
Debut built on loud guitar, feedback and Keith Moon's drumming, including the title track.
Solo acoustic debut showcasing intricate fingerpicked guitar and bleak original songs.
Brisk pop songs on one side, more introspective ballads on the other.
Raw, distorted Northwest garage rock with screamed vocals, including The Witch and Psycho.
Live Chicago club recording of B.B. King's guitar and crowd interaction.
Debut pairing Dylan songs with chiming twelve-string guitar and layered harmonies.
Stax album of originals and covers including I've Been Loving You Too Long and Respect.
Four-part devotional suite by Coltrane's classic quartet.
More introspective Beatles songwriting with folk-rock textures and sitar on Norwegian Wood.
Double album recorded with Nashville session players, known for its thin, wild mercury sound.
Debut built on layered harmonies, including California Dreamin' and Monday, Monday.
First Stones album of all original songs, with Brian Jones adding marimba, sitar and dulcimer.
British blues album showcasing Eric Clapton's loud, sustained Les Paul tone.
Garage pop album including Kicks, an early anti-drug pop hit.
Donovan's shift into psychedelia with Indian and jazz textures, including Season of the Witch.
Mixes frantic garage rock like 7 and 7 Is with baroque pop and a side-long jam.
Early psychedelic album with Roky Erickson's howl and an electric jug, including You're Gonna Miss Me.
Only Yardbirds studio album of all originals, featuring Jeff Beck's inventive guitar.
Brian Wilson's lushly orchestrated album of adolescent longing, including God Only Knows.
Byrds move into psychedelia with Coltrane-inspired guitar on Eight Miles High.
Zappa's double-album debut mixing doo-wop parody, social satire and sound collage.
Close-harmony folk pop including Scarborough Fair/Canticle and Homeward Bound.
Former US soldiers in Germany playing repetitive, abrasive beat music with electric banjo.
Ray Davies's sharply observed character songs about English life, including Sunny Afternoon.
Nina Simone collection of ballads and blues, including the title track and Four Women.
Studio experiments with tape loops, backwards guitar and sitar, ending with Tomorrow Never Knows.
Loretta Lynn's honky tonk album of assertive songs about marriage, led by the title track.
Merle Haggard's songs of prison, wandering and regret, including the title track.
Organ-led blue-eyed soul including the relaxed summer hit Groovin'.
First Monkees album on which the band played most of their own instruments.
Orchestrated, introspective folk rock with surreal character-driven songs.
Bay Area psychedelia with swirling organ and hazy, drug-inspired songs.
Sinatra croons Jobim's bossa nova songs over hushed arrangements by Claus Ogerman.
Garage psychedelia with heavy guitar effects, including I Had Too Much to Dream Last Night.
Concept album styled as a pirate radio broadcast with mock adverts, including I Can See for Miles.
Soft bossa nova pop sung in Astrud Gilberto's cool, understated voice.
Captain Beefheart's debut of warped Delta blues and R&B, with Ry Cooder on guitar.
Syd Barrett-led debut mixing childlike whimsy with extended space jams like Interstellar Overdrive.
Deep baritone folk songs from Fred Neil, including Everybody's Talkin'.
Gentle, very English Kinks songs, ending with Waterloo Sunset.
San Francisco psychedelia led by Grace Slick, including White Rabbit and Somebody to Love.
Tim Buckley's ambitious second album of elaborate, orchestrated folk with soaring vocals.
Varied songs split between Stephen Stills, Neil Young and Richie Furay, including Expecting to Fly.
Nico's deadpan voice over strings and flute, with songs by Jackson Browne, Lou Reed and Dylan.
Arthur Lee's orchestrated acoustic songs with mariachi brass and darkly surreal themes.
Debut built on three interlocking guitars and shared lead vocals, including Omaha.
Leonard Cohen's sparse debut of literary songs, including Suzanne and So Long, Marianne.
Byrds mix country, jazz and psychedelia, including So You Want to Be a Rock 'n' Roll Star.
Organ-driven debut with Jim Morrison's baritone, including Light My Fire and The End.
Hendrix's second album, more melodic and studio-shaped, including Little Wing.
Debut showcasing Hendrix's fuzz and feedback guitar, including Purple Haze and Foxy Lady.
Power trio psychedelia with Clapton's fuzz and wah, including Sunshine of Your Love.
Aretha's Atlantic breakthrough with Muscle Shoals players, including Respect.
Studio-built album framed as a fictional band's show, ending with A Day in the Life.
Drone, noise and stark pop about street life, featuring Nico, produced by Andy Warhol.
Free-flowing, jazz-backed song cycle of memory and longing.
Voodoo-themed swamp psychedelia blending New Orleans R&B with chanting and percussion.
Known for its seventeen-minute title track with organ and drum solos.
Byrds turn to traditional country with Gram Parsons, recorded partly in Nashville.
Eclectic acid folk built on many world instruments and freewheeling song structures.
Extremely loud power trio blues, including a distorted cover of Summertime Blues.
Stones return to blues and country roots, including Sympathy for the Devil.
Half mod rock, half fairy-tale narrated in Stanley Unwin's comic gobbledygook.
Heavy blues rock with Rod Stewart's vocals and Jeff Beck's inventive guitar.
Tropicalia landmark mixing Brazilian song with psychedelic rock and orchestral arrangements.
Live concert recorded for inmates in a California prison.
Song cycle about youth to old age, including America and Mrs. Robinson.
Janis Joplin's raw, ragged vocals over loose psychedelic blues, including Piece of My Heart.
Piano-led song cycle blending soul, gospel and Broadway with abrupt tempo shifts.
Debut mixing Brazilian pop, psychedelia and sound effects with tropicalia playfulness.
Scott Walker's baritone over lush orchestration, including several Jacques Brel covers.
Concept album celebrating a vanishing English village life.
Studio-crafted Byrds album blending country, psychedelia and early Moog synthesizer.
Second Traffic album mixing Steve Winwood's soulful rock with Dave Mason's folk-pop.
Zappa's satire of hippie culture and Sgt. Pepper, built on heavy tape editing.
Distorted, feedback-heavy album ending with the seventeen-minute Sister Ray.
Mellotron-laced harmony pop recorded at Abbey Road, including Time of the Season.
Concept album of raga pieces evoking a day in the Kashmir valley.
Hendrix's sprawling double album, including All Along the Watchtower and Voodoo Child.
Aretha at full power, including Chain of Fools and (You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman.
Sprawling double album jumping between hard rock, folk, music hall and sound collage.
Guitar-free psychedelia built on homemade electronics, violin and Dorothy Moskowitz's vocals.
Rustic debut of gospel, country and soul-tinged rock, including The Weight.
Early rock opera following one man's life from birth to disillusionment.
Dusty Springfield's Atlantic soul album, including Son of a Preacher Man.
Elvis's Memphis comeback sessions blending country and soul, including In the Ghetto.
Traditional folk songs reworked with jazz rhythm section and intricate dual acoustic guitars.
Mostly live album of extended guitar jams built around Bo Diddley's Who Do You Love.
